nuance.usage_note: Americans use robustly often in business and news, as in 'the economy grew robustly' or 'the model performed robustly.' It is more formal than 'strongly' and is often used to suggest resilience, not just force. In casual talk people more often say 'really solid' or 'pretty strong.'

distinctions.note: Strongly emphasizes force or intensity; robustly emphasizes sturdiness and resilience.
Firmly suggests stability or determination, while robustly suggests vigorous health or reliability.

examples.everyday: The new hiking boots are built robustly enough to handle gravel roads and wet creek crossings.
examples.professional: The model performed robustly across all three test sets, so we can move it into production.
examples.analytical: The argument holds robustly even when we relax the assumption of independence, which strengthens the inference.

nuance.analogy: Acting robustly is like a sturdy oak that bends in a storm but does not snap.
nuance.etymology: Formed from robust with the adverb suffix -ly; robust comes from Latin robustus, strong or oak-like.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, 'ROH-bust-lee', instead of the second.
Using robustly for physical force in casual talk where strongly or hard is more natural.

senses.definition: A curved piece of wood attached to the bottom of a rocking chair or cradle that enables it to rock back and forth.
A rocking chair.
The lengthwise curvature of a surfboard. (More rocker is a more curved board.)
senses.example: All modern surfboards share a similar rocker design — Bruce Jones

senses.definition: The breve below as in ḫ.
Someone passionate about rock music.
senses.example: He's been a rocker since high school, filling his room with vinyl records from the seventies.

senses.definition: A musician who plays rock music.
senses.example: The rocker played his guitar with a fierce energy that thrilled the small crowd.

senses.definition: A rock music song.
senses.example: The band closed their set with a loud rocker that the whole audience sang along to.

senses.definition: One who rocks something.
senses.example: She was the best rocker of crying babies on our street.

senses.definition: Any implement or machine working with a rocking motion, such as a trough mounted on rockers for separating gold dust from gravel, etc. by agitation in water.
senses.example: The miners used a rocker to separate gold dust from gravel by shaking it in water.

senses.definition: A tool with small teeth that roughens a metal plate to produce tonality in mezzotints.
senses.example: The engraver ran the rocker across the copper plate to prepare it for printing.

senses.definition: A rocking horse.
A rocker board.
senses.example: Physical therapy included standing on a rocker to strengthen my ankles and balance.

senses.definition: A skate with a curved blade, somewhat resembling in shape the rocker of a cradle.
senses.example: The figure skater glided across the ice on a rocker blade with a graceful curve.

senses.definition: A kind of electrical switch with a spring-loaded actuator.
senses.example: The electrician replaced the old rocker switch on the wall with a modern toggle.

senses.definition: A rock shaft.
senses.example: The engine linkage used a rocker to transfer motion from the cam to the valves.

senses.definition: A curved line accompanying the chevrons that denote rank, qualifying the rank with a grade.
senses.example: The sergeant's sleeve showed three chevrons with a rocker, marking him as a senior sergeant.

core.definition: A rocking chair, or the curved wooden runner on the bottom of a rocking chair or cradle that lets it move back and forth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAH. The final -er is an r-colored syllable, so don't say it as 'rock-ah'. The vowel in the first syllable is the open ah of 'lot.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and homey when describing furniture. Other senses, such as a rock music fan, are casual slang.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, rocker often means the whole rocking chair, especially on a porch. Furniture makers may use it for the curved runner itself. Rocker is also slang for a rock musician or fan, and it appears in surfing for a board's curve. A natural remark is 'Mind if I grab the rocker?'

distinctions.note: Rocking chair is the standard full phrase for the chair; rocker is shorter and common in everyday speech, but in furniture talk it can mean just the curved runner.
A glider moves forward and back on a sliding frame instead of curved runners, so it has no rockers.

examples.everyday: Grandma likes to sit in the rocker on the porch every evening.
examples.professional: The furniture catalog lists the rocker in oak and walnut, with a glider option for smaller spaces.
examples.analytical: The rocker's curved runner turns a simple back-and-forth motion into a rhythm that feels calming and self-soothing.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat hull rocking gently on waves, the curved runner lets the chair sway without tipping over.
nuance.etymology: From the verb rock plus the agent suffix -er, meaning something that rocks.
common_mistakes: Calling the whole chair a rocker when the speaker means a rocking chair in a formal context; use rocking chair for clarity.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a separate 'ah' sound instead of an r-colored -er.

core.definition: The capital city of Italy and, in biblical times, the capital of the Roman Empire, where Paul was taken as a prisoner and wrote letters to Christians.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one stressed syllable, with a clear American r and a long o; do not add a second syllable. Non-native speakers often stress it wrongly or pronounce a flat ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious contexts it can also carry weight as the historic center of the Western church, depending on the speaker's tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Rome for the Italian city in everyday travel talk, and for the ancient empire in history and Bible study. In church settings, saying the Church of Rome or the see of Rome usually refers to the Roman Catholic Church and its papacy, so context matters.
word_family: Romans (noun, a book of the New Testament)

distinctions.note: Rome is the city or place; Roman describes people, things or customs from Rome, such as Roman law or a Roman Catholic.

examples.everyday: We're flying to Rome this summer, so I'm finally practicing my Italian.
examples.professional: The Rome office will take over the translation project next quarter.
examples.analytical: Paul's letter to the believers in Rome shaped how later Christians understood justification by faith.

nuance.analogy: Rome is like a name that stands for both a city on a map and a whole system of power and religious authority, depending on how it is used.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Roma, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying ROH-muh with an extra syllable; the word is one syllable.
Confusing Rome, the city, with Roman, the adjective: say Roman food, but Rome is the city.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek the city is called Rhōmē, the capital of the Roman Empire in New Testament times. Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome at Pentecost. Acts 28:16 describes Paul arriving in Rome as a prisoner, where he was allowed to live under guard in his own lodging. Romans 1:7 shows Paul addressing his letter to the believers living in Rome.

traditions.view: Rome is the see of the Bishop of Rome, the pope, whom Catholics regard as the successor of Peter with universal authority in the Church.
Orthodox Christians historically honored the bishop of Rome as first in honor among the patriarchs, but reject the claim of universal papal jurisdiction over the whole Church.
Most Protestants reject papal supremacy and the idea that Rome holds unique authority over the Church, though Lutherans, Reformed, Anglicans and Baptists differ in how they assess the historic see.

senses.definition: An act of rubbing.
senses.example: Give that lamp a good rub and see if any genies come out.

senses.definition: A difficulty or problem.
senses.example: The real rub is that the new software costs twice as much as the old one.

senses.definition: In the game of crown green bowls, any obstacle by which a bowl is diverted from its normal course.
senses.example: A rub on the green sent my bowl wide of the jack, costing me the end.

senses.definition: Any substance designed to be applied by rubbing.
senses.example: a heat rub intended for muscular strains

senses.definition: A mixture of spices applied to meat before it is barbecued.
senses.example: Her secret barbecue rub includes smoked paprika, brown sugar, and a little cayenne.

senses.definition: To move (one object) while maintaining contact with another object over some area, with pressure and friction.
senses.example: I rubbed the cloth over the glass.

senses.definition: To be rubbed against something.
senses.example: My shoes are beginning to rub.

senses.definition: To spread a substance thinly over; to smear.
senses.example: meat rubbed with spices before barbecuing

senses.definition: To scour; to burnish; to polish; to brighten; to cleanse; often with up or over.
senses.example: to rub up silver

senses.definition: To hinder; to cross; to thwart.
senses.example: Bad luck seemed to rub every plan we made for the summer.

senses.definition: To touch the jack with the bowl.
senses.example: His final bowl rubbed the jack and stopped right beside it on the green.

senses.definition: (dated) To move or pass with difficulty.
senses.example: to rub through woods, as huntsmen
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To move your hand or an object back and forth over a surface with firm pressure.

pronunciation.tip: Short 'uh' vowel, like 'cup'. Pronounce the final b clearly, without adding an extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an everyday physical action, though it can suggest comfort when used for massage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'rub' for massaging or smoothing lotion, as in 'rub some cream on the sunburn.' In sports or work talk, 'the rub' means the difficulty. The idiom 'there's the rub' means the real problem is this.

distinctions.note: 'Scrub' means to clean firmly with a brush or cloth, while 'rub' is gentler and general.
'Massage' is a deliberate therapeutic or relaxing treatment; 'rub' is general and informal.

examples.everyday: Can you rub some sunscreen on my back before we go to the beach?
examples.professional: I rubbed the spreadsheet cells to clean up the formatting before sending the report.
examples.analytical: The argument rubs against the grain of the earlier text in a way that exposes an unresolved tension.

nuance.analogy: Like smoothing a wrinkle out of a shirt with your hand.
common_mistakes: Using 'rub' for cleaning; Americans often say 'scrub' or 'wipe' for cleaning.
Confusing 'rub it in' with 'rub off' in idioms.

rub.etymology: Middle English *rubben*, of origin; possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic, a hypothetical variant of **ruppōną* (“to tear, rip; to wear away, rub”), related to **reufaną* (“to tear”) (> *reave*).

senses.definition: To become exhausted. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see run out,‎ out of,‎ gas.
senses.example: We ran out of gas on the highway, so we walked two miles to the station.

core.definition: To use up all the fuel in a vehicle; figuratively, to become exhausted or lose energy and motivation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on GAS, the last word, with a lighter stress on RUN and OUT. The word 'of' reduces to a weak 'uhv', and the 'ow' in 'out' is a diphthong, not a pure vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the literal sense; mildly negative when used about a person, suggesting they are worn out or have no energy left.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this literally about cars and figuratively about people, as in 'I'm running out of gas after that long hike.' It is very common in casual conversation. A natural reply is 'Me too, let's stop for coffee.' For a more formal context, say 'I'm exhausted' or 'I'm running low on energy.'

distinctions.note: 'Run low' means the supply is getting small and is used for things like money or groceries; 'run out of gas' implies the supply is completely gone or that someone is exhausted.
'Burn out' describes long-term exhaustion from stress or overwork, while 'run out of gas' is a more temporary, everyday tiredness.

collocations: run out of gas on the highway
run out of gas halfway through the day
run out of gas before the finish line

examples.everyday: We almost ran out of gas on the way to the lake, so we stopped at the next station.
examples.professional: After three back-to-back sprints, the team is running out of gas, so let's push the launch to next month.
examples.analytical: A theory that runs out of gas after a few explanatory successes may still be useful, but its reach is clearly limited.

nuance.analogy: Like a car's fuel gauge hitting empty, a person's energy can drop suddenly when the reserves are used up.
common_mistakes: Saying 'run out gas' without the preposition 'of'.
Using it for a person who is only slightly tired; it suggests more complete exhaustion.

conversation.text: We ran out of gas two miles from the next exit.
Fill up now so we don't run out of gas in the desert.
I ran out of gas by the end of the day and needed a nap.

senses.definition: To be the leader, to be in charge.

core.definition: To be the person in charge of an organization, event or group, making the important decisions and directing others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SHOH, the last word. The is reduced to a weak thuh before a consonant, and show rhymes with go, not with shower.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for competence; it can sound negative if the person seems bossy or controlling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for a person who directs a project, a household, a team or a family event: 'Who's running the show at the office this week?' It is informal and friendly, not a technical job title. A natural reply is a short acknowledgment such as 'Right, Dana runs the show,' or a question like 'So who do I talk to?'

distinctions.note: Be in charge is neutral and suitable for any setting; run the show is more informal and emphasizes hands-on, day-to-day control.
Call the shots is very close in meaning and often stresses making the final decisions, especially when others would prefer otherwise.
Take charge describes the act of beginning to lead, often in an emergency; run the show describes a continuing role.

collocations: run the show at the office
run the show on game night
run the show for the team

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the barbecue; my aunt runs the show every year, so she'll tell us where to stand.
examples.professional: Dana runs the show on this project, so send the schedule changes to her rather than to me.
examples.analytical: Whoever runs the show in a bureaucracy often holds less formal authority than the people who write its rules, yet exercises more practical power.

nuance.analogy: Like a conductor who keeps the orchestra together: the musicians play, but the conductor sets the tempo and gives the cues.
nuance.etymology: Run from Old English rinnan; show from Old English scēawian (to look at). The idiom's exact origin is not firmly documented.
common_mistakes: Saying run the show of the event instead of run the show for the event or simply run the show.
Using the formal word administrate in casual speech; Americans say run the show.
Pronouncing the as thee before a consonant; it is thuh before a consonant.

senses.definition: To make sacred.

core.definition: To make something sacred, or to treat a person, place, or idea as sacred and beyond criticism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final '-ize' as 'eyez' in American speech. The middle syllables are reduced, so 'kruh' is short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly writing; it can carry a critical edge when used to describe political or social reverence.
nuance.usage_note: Sacralize is mainly used in academic writing about religion, sociology, and politics, such as discussing how a nation or leader is treated as sacred. Everyday American speakers usually say treat as sacred or make sacred instead. Spell it with a z, since American English uses sacralize rather than sacralise.

distinctions.note: Sanctify is a theological term for making holy, often by divine action, while sacralize describes humans or societies treating something as sacred.
Consecrate refers to a formal ritual that sets something apart for sacred use, whereas sacralize is a broader process of social or cultural reverence.

examples.everyday: My dad pretty much sacralizes his old pickup, and nobody is allowed to touch it.
examples.professional: The style guide should not sacralize the legacy templates, since we can revise them when the brand changes.
examples.analytical: Durkheim argues that societies sacralize their collective symbols, making them objects of shared reverence and moral obligation.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a family heirloom under glass, sacralizing removes something from ordinary use and wraps it in reverence.
nuance.etymology: From sacred plus the suffix -ize, from Latin sacer (holy, sacred).
common_mistakes: Using sacralize in casual speech where treat as sacred sounds more natural.
Spelling it sacralise, which is the British form.

senses.definition: An unhappy or disappointed person.

core.definition: An informal, playful name for someone who looks or feels unhappy, disappointed or grumpy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word panda, with the main stress on PAN, and say the first word sad with a lighter stress. The final -a is a reduced uh sound, not the Spanish-style ah.

nuance.connotation: Playful and lighthearted, sometimes teasing; it is rarely hurtful unless used to mock someone who is genuinely upset.
nuance.usage_note: Americans, especially younger people and online communities, use this phrase to tease a friend who is moping, sulking or looking down. Common phrases include Don't be a sad panda and Why the sad panda face? A good reply is something like Sorry, I'm just tired, or a laugh followed by a cheerful change of subject. Avoid it with a boss, a customer or anyone who is actually grieving.

distinctions.note: Sad panda is playful and used for temporary moods, while sad sack is a more contemptuous label for a chronically inept or unlucky person.
A grump is a bad-tempered person, while a sad panda is mainly sad or disappointed, and the phrase is much lighter.
Sadness is a plain emotional noun, while sad panda is a humorous, informal label used in conversation.

examples.everyday: Come on, don't be a sad panda, we still have time to get pizza before the movie starts.
examples.professional: Sorry I was a sad panda in the standup, I'm just worried about the deadline for the migration.
examples.analytical: Calling the defeated candidate a sad panda trivializes the serious grievances that actually drove her supporters' disappointment.

nuance.analogy: Like a cartoon character with a droopy face who never quite wins at anything, but whom everyone secretly likes.
common_mistakes: Using sad panda in serious situations, where it can sound dismissive or mocking.
Pronouncing panda with the Spanish-style pan-DAH instead of PAN-duh.

sad-panda.etymology: From Sexual Harassment Panda, an episode in 1999 of the animated comedy series South Park.

senses.definition: In a sad manner; sorrowfully.
senses.example: “Only when we climb up can we see it,” he said sadly.

senses.definition: Unfortunately, sad to say.
senses.example: If you think you’re getting out of this place alive, you are sadly mistaken, my friend.

senses.definition: In a manner to cause sadness; badly; terribly.
senses.example: The old bridge was sadly neglected, with rusted railings and cracked concrete everywhere.

senses.definition: (dated) Very much (of a desire etc.); dearly; urgently.
senses.example: Sir, I sadly wish to hear your sermon again before I leave.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Unfortunately; used to say that something is regrettable or disappointing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the a short, as in bad, not as in say. The final -ly is a light lee, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild: it signals regret about bad news, often with a shrug or a sigh.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, sadly most often means unfortunately and comes at the start of a sentence, as in Sadly, the bakery closed. People use it when sharing bad news or expressing regret. In formal business writing, unfortunately is more common. The older sense, in a sad manner, appears mainly in literary writing, as in she sighed sadly.

distinctions.note: They are nearly interchangeable as sentence adverbs; sadly carries more feeling, while unfortunately is more neutral and common in business.
Sad is an adjective; sadly describes how something is done or introduces a regretful comment.

examples.everyday: Sadly, we're out of the blueberry muffins, but the lemon ones are great.
examples.professional: Sadly, the vendor cannot meet the March deadline, so we need to revise the project plan.
examples.analytical: Sadly, the argument assumes what it sets out to prove, so it cannot establish its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a soft sigh placed before bad news, which softens the sentence that follows.
nuance.etymology: From sad (Old English sæd, meaning sated or weary) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Saying I feel sadly instead of I feel sad; after feel, use the adjective sad.
Using sadly to mean sad in describing a person, as in a sadly man, instead of a sad man.

senses.definition: Carnal, fleshly.
Designating the lowest level of human thought; focused on neither intellectual (psychic) nor spiritual (pneumatic) reality.

core.definition: Relating to the flesh or bodily appetites rather than the mind or spirit; in some ancient Christian thought, the lowest level of human nature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ar' is the American vowel of 'car' with a clear r. The ending is a short 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in tone because it ranks bodily life as the lowest level; it is a technical label in religious study rather than a casual insult.
nuance.usage_note: Sarkic is a specialized term used mainly in theology, patristics and the history of religion, not in everyday talk. Americans would meet it in a seminary course or a book on early Christian or Gnostic anthropology. In ordinary conversation it sounds pretentious, so say 'carnal' or 'fleshly' instead.

distinctions.note: Carnal is ordinary English for bodily or sexual desire; sarkic is a technical theological term for the flesh level of human nature.
In the same three-level scheme, psychic names the soulish middle level, while sarkic names the lowest and most purely bodily level.

examples.professional: In my seminar paper I used Irenaeus's report of the Valentinian triad, with its sarkic, psychic and pneumatic levels, to frame the anthropology.
examples.analytical: Paul's contrast between living according to the flesh and living by the Spirit is sometimes read as a sarkic and pneumatic binary, though he never sets out a three-tier scheme.

nuance.analogy: Think of it as the basement of a three-floor house: the body's appetites sit there, below the mind and the spirit.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sarkikos, 'of the flesh,' from sarx, 'flesh'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long a or as 'sar-keek'; the first vowel is open and the stress is on the first syllable.
Using it as a synonym for 'sarcastic' or 'sarcasm', which are unrelated words.
nuance.biblical_note: The three-level scheme behind sarkic is not in Scripture; it comes from later Christian and Gnostic writing. The biblical root is Paul's Greek sarx, 'flesh,' and sarkikos, 'fleshly.' In 1 Corinthians 2:14 Paul contrasts the natural person with the spiritual person. In 1 Corinthians 3:1-3 he says the Corinthians are still fleshly and not ready for solid food. In Romans 8:6 he says that a mind set on the flesh leads to death, while a mind set on the Spirit leads to life and peace.

senses.definition: To only afford the essentials; to barely sustain oneself.
senses.example: Everyone in her family had to get a second job just so they could scrape by.

core.definition: To manage to get enough money for basic needs, with very little left over for anything else.

pronunciation.tip: In American speech the main stress falls on BY, the particle, not on scrape, so say skrayp-BY. Link the final p of scrape smoothly into the b of by, so it sounds like skray-PBY, with no pause between the words.

nuance.connotation: Negative or sympathetic. It implies hardship and a narrow margin, so it describes difficulty rather than comfort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scrape by for households, students, or small businesses that are short of money but are still covering rent and food. It is informal and is often used in conversation about the economy, jobs, or personal finances. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it's been tight, but we're managing,' which suggests you are not in crisis.

distinctions.note: Get by is neutral and can mean simply coping with what you have, while scrape by stresses how little margin there is.
Make ends meet is a common idiom about balancing income and expenses, and it is more neutral; scrape by emphasizes the struggle and the thin margin.
Scrape through means to pass or succeed narrowly, such as an exam, not to survive financially.

collocations: scrape by after losing a job

examples.everyday: After the layoff we scraped by on savings until he found a new job.
examples.professional: The nonprofit has been scraping by on grants, so the new hire will have to wait until the next funding round.
examples.analytical: Many households in the study merely scrape by, with income covering necessities but leaving no margin for emergencies.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat that stays afloat by bailing water as fast as it comes in.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English scrapen, probably from Old Norse skrapa, 'to scrape'.
common_mistakes: Stressing scrape instead of by, which makes the phrase sound like a single verb.
Using scrape by to mean succeed narrowly, which is scrape through in standard American usage.

senses.definition: A person who disposes of scraps, such as one who collects scrap metal to sell to a scrap dealer.
senses.example: After the uncle died they sold off most of his rustbuckets to a scrapper and kept one to fix up.

senses.definition: A person who fights doggedly, who exhibits indomitable will.
senses.example: He's a real scrapper, even against impossible odds, he always keeps fighting.

core.definition: A person who is tough, determined, and will fight hard to succeed, even when the odds are against them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SKRAP, and the word has only one p in the standard spelling and pronunciation. The final er is a short rhotic syllable, not a long vowel. Learners often pronounce an extra p sound, so keep the middle as a single p.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises determination and grit, especially in someone who started with few advantages.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scrapper to admire someone who refuses to quit, often in sports, business, or a young person who overcomes hardship. It is informal and a little folksy, so it fits conversation better than formal writing. A natural reply is 'Yeah, she's a real scrapper,' often with a smile of respect.

distinctions.note: Fighter can be literal or neutral, while scrapper stresses scrappy, scrappy, and underdog persistence.
A scrap dealer buys and sells scrap metal for a living, which is a rare or technical sense of scrapper, not the everyday one.

examples.everyday: Don't count her out, she's a scrapper and always finds a way through.
examples.professional: Our small team is full of scrappers who will find a way to ship the release even with a short budget.
examples.analytical: The novel's protagonist is a scrapper whose persistence turns hardship into a form of moral dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like a boxer who keeps getting up after every round.
nuance.etymology: From scrap (to fight, to scuffle) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using scrapper for a person who collects scrap metal, which is a rare and technical sense.
Pronouncing the middle as a double p sound, which is not standard in American speech.

senses.definition: The act or sound of something being scratched.
senses.example: We heard further scratchings at the door as the dog whined to be let in.

senses.definition: A pork scratching.
Record scratching, a technique of starting and stopping a vinyl record from playing to produce music in hip hop.
senses.example: The DJ's scratching over the breakbeat had the whole club on its feet.

core.definition: The act or sound of scratching a surface, skin, or object, such as an animal's claws or a pen moving across paper.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ing is a short ih sound, not a long ee, so do not stretch it into 'SKRACH-eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word for an action or sound, though it can feel unpleasant when the sound is grating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scratching in everyday talk for sounds at doors, walls, or attics, as in 'I hear scratching in the attic.' In British food talk, pork scratchings are a snack, but Americans say pork rinds. Record scratching is a term from hip hop. A natural reply to a noise is 'It's probably the cat.'

distinctions.note: Scraping means pushing a hard edge across a surface to remove something, while scratching is lighter and leaves marks or sounds.
Itching is the sensation; scratching is the action of rubbing the skin to relieve it.

examples.everyday: There's scratching in the attic again, so it's probably a raccoon.
examples.professional: The scratching noise in the server room turned out to be a loose fan blade.
examples.analytical: The scratching of the pen across the page was the only sound in the empty library.

nuance.analogy: Like a fingernail on a chalkboard: a sharp, repeated sound that draws attention.
nuance.etymology: From the verb scratch with the -ing suffix forming a noun of action.
common_mistakes: Using scratching in British food contexts for pork rinds; Americans say pork rinds.
Confusing scratching, the act or sound, with scratch, a mark or small cut on a surface.

senses.definition: To convert assets or claims (typically outstanding loans or other receivables) to securities, usually by selling them with a discount to a financial intermediary, which pools them with other similar assets and sells further as securities to third-party investors.
senses.example: The bank planned to securitize its auto loans and sell them to investors through a trust.

core.definition: To convert loans or other receivables into tradable securities by pooling them and selling them to investors.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KYUR, and the final '-ize' is a secondary stress pronounced 'tyze', rhyming with 'eyes'. Do not reduce the 'ize' to 'uhz', and keep the r in KYUR clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in finance, but associated with the 2008 financial crisis, when pooling loans was criticized for hiding risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in finance, banking and economics, especially with mortgages, auto loans and student loans. In casual talk it is jargon, so most people would say 'bundle' or 'package' loans instead. It became widely discussed after the 2008 crisis.

distinctions.note: Issuing bonds creates new debt directly, while securitizing converts existing loans or receivables into securities.
Secure means to make safe or to obtain something, while securitize specifically means to turn assets into tradable securities.

examples.everyday: My cousin works at a bank, and she said they bundle and securitize car loans before selling them to investors.
examples.professional: The fund plans to securitize its consumer loan portfolio next quarter to free up capital.
examples.analytical: Banks that securitize loans can move credit risk off their balance sheets, though that transfer may weaken underwriting standards.

nuance.analogy: To securitize loans is like pouring many small streams of water into one pipe and selling shares of the flow.
nuance.etymology: From 'security' (from Latin securitas, 'freedom from care') plus the suffix '-ize', 'to make into'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the last syllable, as in 'sih-kyoo-ruh-TYZE'
Confusing 'securitize' with 'secure', which means to make safe or protected

senses.definition: One who is involved in sedition.

core.definition: A person who incites or takes part in rebellion against a government, usually through speech, writing, or organized action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the first syllable is weak. Do not stress the first syllable as SEH-dish-un-ist.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It is usually used as an accusation, and whoever says it is making a serious charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seditionist mostly in politics, news, and legal discussion. Calling someone a seditionist is a strong accusation, so people often prefer more specific terms such as insurrectionist or traitor. In everyday talk it may sound heated or dramatic.

distinctions.note: A traitor betrays a country, often by helping an enemy, while a seditionist stirs up rebellion against the government from within.
An insurrectionist takes part in an armed uprising, while a seditionist may act only through speech or writing.
A dissident openly disagrees with authorities, usually within the law, while a seditionist incites rebellion against them.

examples.everyday: My uncle calls those protesters seditionists, but I think they're just angry about prices.
examples.professional: The policy team avoided calling any critic a seditionist, since that word is a legal accusation rather than a description.
examples.analytical: The regime treated every reformer as a seditionist, erasing the line between criticism and conspiracy.

nuance.analogy: A seditionist is like a spark near a gas line: the danger is not talk alone but the moment it ignites a crowd against authority.
nuance.etymology: From sedition, from Latin seditio, a going apart or discord, from sed-, apart, and itio, a going.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second, as in SEH-dish-un-ist.
Using seditionist as a neutral word for any protester, when it is a serious accusation.

senses.definition: Of, related to, or being involved in sedition.
senses.example: The pamphlet was deemed seditious by the colonial governor, who ordered every copy seized.

core.definition: Describing speech, writing or action that encourages rebellion or disorder against the government or authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on DISH, and the final syllable is a light 'us' sound. Keep the first vowel weak, so it sounds like 'suh' rather than 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; suggests a dangerous or subversive act, and is often used to attack opponents.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seditious in legal and political writing, news reports and history. Many Americans would not use it in casual talk, where they would say 'subversive' or 'inflammatory' instead. It sounds stiff in everyday speech, so reserve it for serious contexts.

distinctions.note: Subversive is broader and can describe quiet undermining of institutions, while seditious specifically concerns incitement to revolt.
Inflammatory describes language that provokes anger, while seditious describes language that encourages rebellion against authority.

examples.everyday: The news said the pamphlets were seditious, but my neighbor just thought they were rude.
examples.professional: Compliance flagged the internal memo as seditious because it called on employees to ignore the directives of leadership.
examples.analytical: Whether a pamphlet is seditious depends less on its anger than on whether it calls for resistance to the lawful order.

nuance.analogy: Like a spark near a fuel tank: the spark itself is small, but its purpose is to set off an explosion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin seditiosus, from seditio 'discord, mutiny'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in 'SED-ih-shus'.
Confusing it with 'seductive', which has a different meaning and pronunciation.

senses.definition: The act of seducing.
senses.example: Seduction is the fine art of manipulating people based on physical attraction and desire. Step 1: Be attractive. Step 2: Don't be unattractive.

senses.definition: A seductive aspect of something; appeal.
senses.example: The seduction of easy money drew many young traders into risky investments.

core.definition: The act of persuading or attracting someone, often sexually, through charm or temptation, or the strong appeal of something tempting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, with a short u sound as in cup. The ending -tion is pronounced shun, and the final n is often syllabic, so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. Used literally it can suggest manipulation, and used figuratively it can be playful or simply describe strong appeal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seduction both literally and figuratively, as in the seduction of easy money. In casual talk it is often used for advertising or temptation, such as a shop's seduction of sales. For ordinary flirting Americans usually say flirting or hitting on someone, and seduction sounds more dramatic or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Temptation is the desire to do something wrong or unwise, while seduction stresses the attraction and persuasion that create that desire.
Flirtation is light and playful, while seduction implies a deliberate effort to win someone over.
Enticement is the attraction that draws someone toward something, and it is usually less manipulative than seduction.

examples.everyday: The new phone ads are pure seduction, but I'm trying not to buy something I don't need.
examples.professional: The sales team's pitch relied on the seduction of quick returns, which made the risks easy to overlook.
examples.analytical: Augustine's Confessions shows how a small desire can gradually bind the will, as the seduction of sin works through habit.

nuance.analogy: Seduction is like a slow tide: it does not pull you under at once, but it steadily carries you away from the shore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin seductio, a leading aside, from seducere, to lead aside.
common_mistakes: Using seduction as a neutral word for attraction in serious or professional contexts, where it can sound inappropriate.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second, as in SEE-duk-shun.
nuance.biblical_note: Exodus 22:16 in the Revised Standard Version addresses a man who seduces a virgin who is not betrothed, requiring him to pay the bride-price. The Hebrew verb behind this is pata, to entice or persuade. Proverbs 7 describes a young man led astray by a woman's smooth words, warning that he follows her as an ox goes to the slaughter. The chapter presents seduction as a path that leads to ruin.

seduction.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *séduction*, from Latin *sēductiō*, from *sēdūcō*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to seed or semen.
senses.example: The botanist studied the seminal structures of the plant's cones.

senses.definition: Creative or having the power to originate.
senses.example: Darwin's book was seminal, reshaping biology and inspiring generations of scientists.

senses.definition: Highly influential, especially in some original way, and providing a basis for future development or research.
senses.example: "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" was a seminal work in the modern philosophy of science.

core.definition: Highly influential, and providing the original basis for later development or research in a field.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEM. The second and third syllables are reduced, so it sounds like "SEM-ih-nul," with no strong vowel in the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises work that founded or transformed a field.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "seminal" in academic, professional, and journalistic writing to praise a foundational work, paper, or idea. In casual talk, it can sound a bit formal or self-consciously intellectual. Its literal sense about seed is rare in everyday American use.

distinctions.note: Influential means having a strong effect; seminal adds that the work originated something new that others built on.
Important is general and neutral; seminal is specific and praises a foundational origin.

examples.everyday: My professor called that old album seminal because almost every rock band after it copied its sound.
examples.professional: Her seminal paper on gradient boosting is still cited in almost every modeling guide.
examples.analytical: Augustine's seminal treatment of time in the Confessions shaped the subsequent history of Western philosophy.

nuance.analogy: A seminal work is like a seed: small at the start, but everything later grows from it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sēminālis, "of seed," from sēmen, "seed."
common_mistakes: Using "seminal" for something merely old; it means influential at the origin of a field.
Confusing it with "seminar" in pronunciation or meaning.

seminal.etymology: From Middle English *seminal*, *semynal*, from Old French *seminal*, *seminale*, from Latin *sēminālis*, ultimately from oblique stem of Latin *sēmen* (“seed”) *-al*.

senses.definition: A theological school for the training of rabbis, priests, or ministers.
A private residential school for girls.
senses.example: She was sent to a strict seminary for girls in Virginia, where she learned French and piano.

senses.definition: A class of religious education for youths ages 14–18 that accompanies normal secular education.
senses.example: Every Sunday, the teenagers attended seminary classes before school to study scripture and church history.

senses.definition: A piece of ground where seed is sown for producing plants for transplantation.
senses.example: We sowed lettuce in the seminary before transplanting the seedlings into the garden.

senses.definition: The place or original stock from which anything is brought or produced.
senses.example: Silicon Valley was the seminary of many modern software ideas.

senses.definition: A Roman Catholic priest educated in a foreign seminary; a seminarist.
senses.example: The Irish seminary studied in Rome and then returned to Boston to serve a parish.

senses.definition: Of or relating to seed; seminal.
senses.example: Her seminary ideas about data structures shaped the whole field.

core.definition: A school that trains students, especially future priests, ministers, or rabbis, in religious studies.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEM. The middle syllable is a reduced vowel, and the final syllable is a light "ee," not "ary" with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a serious institution, with no negative sense in religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, "seminary" usually means a graduate school for ministry or priesthood, such as Fuller or Princeton Theological Seminary. Americans also say "divinity school" for some university programs. The older sense of a girls' boarding school is now rare and historical.

distinctions.note: A seminar is a meeting or class for discussion; a seminary is an institution that trains religious leaders.
Divinity school is a common American term for a university-based religious studies school; a seminary is usually independent and focused on ministry.

examples.everyday: My cousin is going to seminary in the fall because she wants to become a pastor.
examples.professional: Our church partners with a seminary to offer online courses for lay leaders.
examples.analytical: The seminary curriculum balances biblical languages, historical theology, and pastoral practice.

nuance.analogy: A seminary is like a medical school for ministers: it teaches the knowledge and the practice needed for the calling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sēminārium, "seedbed," used for a place where young people are trained.
common_mistakes: Confusing seminary with seminar; a seminary is a school, not a meeting.
Stressing the last syllable; keep the stress on SEM.

senses.definition: Things that can be sensed; stimuli.

core.definition: In philosophy, things that can be sensed, including objects not currently perceived, the things that the senses could in principle detect.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the first syllable, SENS, with a secondary stress on the 'bi' syllable. The final 'ia' is a light 'ee-uh' sound. Keep the 'i' in the middle syllables short and reduced, and do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a specialized philosophical term.
nuance.usage_note: Sensibilia is a technical term from ordinary language philosophy, especially J. L. Austin's work on perception. It is a plural noun, and the singular is 'sensibile', which is rarely used. Americans in everyday talk would simply say 'things we can see or hear'.

distinctions.note: Sense data are the mind-dependent objects we are actually aware of, whereas sensibilia are sensible things in general, including those we do not currently perceive.
Sensible as an adjective means able to be perceived by the senses, while sensibilia is a noun for those perceivable things themselves.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor kept talking about sensibilia, and I still do not get the difference from ordinary objects.
examples.professional: In the usability study, we tracked which sensibilia participants noticed on the screen, meaning the visual elements they could perceive.
examples.analytical: Austin argues that the realist's appeal to sensibilia does not refute the skeptic, because the existence of unperceived objects is not what is at issue.

nuance.analogy: Think of sensibilia as the whole station of radio signals the receiver could pick up, while sense data are only the station currently playing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sensibilis 'perceptible by the senses', from sensus 'feeling'; the neuter plural form was adopted into English philosophical use.
common_mistakes: Treating 'sensibilia' as a singular noun; the singular is 'sensibile', and the plural 'sensibilia' takes a plural verb.
Confusing it with 'sensibility', which means emotional sensitivity or taste.

senses.definition: Appealing to the senses, or to sensual gratification.
senses.example: Although we rarely see Casanova himself on our tour of his sensuous world, we feel his presence as we look at paintings, sculpture, snuff boxes, embroidered vests, silk dresses, silver candy dishes, etc.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the senses; sensory.
senses.example: The sensuous texture of the silk scarf made her want to touch it again.

senses.definition: Appreciative of stimulation.
senses.example: I consider myself a sensuous lover.

core.definition: Pleasing to the senses, especially through beauty, texture, sound, or color, often in art, music, or design.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, and the 'sh' sound comes from the 'sue' spelling. Say the final syllable as a reduced 'uhs', not 'us'. Do not confuse it with 'sensual', which has an 'l' ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises beauty and aesthetic pleasure, with less erotic suggestion than 'sensual'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sensuous' mainly in art criticism, poetry, music, and interior or product design, to describe beautiful textures, colors, or sounds. In casual talk it sounds literary, so people often say 'luxurious' or 'soft' instead. It is more aesthetic than 'sensual', so it is safer to use for an artwork or a fabric.

distinctions.note: Sensuous emphasizes aesthetic delight in beauty, while sensual emphasizes bodily or erotic pleasure.
Sensory is a neutral technical term for the senses, while sensuous is an evaluative term praising pleasing sensations.

examples.everyday: The silk scarf has a wonderfully sensuous feel, so I bought it for my sister.
examples.professional: Our packaging should feel sensuous, with soft matte textures and warm colors that invite customers to touch the product.
examples.analytical: Keats's poetry is sensuous, dwelling on color, scent, and touch as the means by which the soul apprehends beauty.

nuance.analogy: A sensuous piece of art is like a ripe peach: the pleasure comes through touch, color, and smell all at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sensus 'feeling, perception', via sensual with the suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Using 'sensuous' and 'sensual' as interchangeable; 'sensuous' is more aesthetic and less erotic.
Stressing the second syllable, which is not natural; the stress falls on SEN.

senses.definition: A general thought, feeling, or sense.
senses.example: The sentiment emerged that we were acting too soon.

senses.definition: Feelings, especially tender feelings, as apart from reason or judgment, or of a weak or foolish kind.
senses.example: Good decision-making is not governed by mere sentiment.

core.definition: A general feeling, opinion, or attitude about something. Often used for the feeling a group or public holds.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SEN. The second syllable is a reduced vowel like 'tuh', and the final -ment is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive, negative, or mixed, depending on context and the attitude described.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sentiment for public opinion or the attitude of a group, as in market sentiment or a shared sentiment. It is also used for tender feelings, but in that sense it can sound slightly old-fashioned or sappy. In business and news, the word is common and neutral.

distinctions.note: Feeling is the everyday word for emotion. Sentiment often refers to an attitude or opinion, especially one shared by a group.
Opinion is a judgment you reason toward. Sentiment is more emotional and may not rest on careful reasoning.
Sentiment can be a normal, appropriate feeling. Sentimentality is an excessive or self-indulgent display of it.

examples.everyday: There's a lot of sentiment against the new parking rules in our neighborhood, so the council may reconsider.
examples.professional: Customer sentiment dropped after the update, so we need to check the support tickets before the next release.
examples.analytical: Hume argues that moral judgments rest on sentiment rather than pure reason, which makes emotional response central to ethics.

nuance.analogy: Sentiment is the weather of opinion: it is felt widely, shifts quickly, and shapes what people do.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sentire, to feel, through Old French and Middle English.
common_mistakes: Using sentiment to mean sentence, which is a different word.
Using sentiment for a single thought when feeling or attitude is the usual meaning.

senses.definition: An ordered list of objects, typically indexed with natural numbers.
A set of things next to each other in a set order; a series.
senses.example: An alphabet follows a sequence.

senses.definition: The state of being sequent or following; order of succession.
senses.example: Complete the listed tasks in sequence.

senses.definition: A series of musical phrases where a theme or melody is repeated, with some change each time, such as in pitch or length (example: opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony).
senses.example: The melody in the second bar is repeated in a higher sequence before the cadence.

senses.definition: A musical composition used in some Catholic Masses between the readings. The most famous sequence is the Dies Irae (Day of Wrath) formerly used in funeral services.
senses.example: The choir sang the Dies Irae sequence before the homily during the Requiem Mass.

senses.definition: A series of shots that depict a single action or style in a film, television show, or other video medium.
senses.example: The montage sequence showed the athlete training through rain, snow, and sunshine.

senses.definition: A meld consisting of three or more cards of successive ranks in the same suit, such as the four, five and six of hearts.
senses.example: I needed a sequence of three hearts to win the hand, but I only had two.

senses.definition: (rare) A subsequent event; a consequence or result.
senses.example: The lost contract was a sequence of the manager's careless budgeting decisions.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To arrange (something) in an order.
senses.example: We sequenced the code to keep it organized.

senses.definition: To determine the order of monomers in (a biological polymer), e.g. of amino acids in (a protein), or of bases in (a nucleic acid).
senses.example: Researchers sequenced the genome of the bacteria to identify the mutation responsible for resistance.

senses.definition: To produce (music) with a sequencer.
senses.example: She sequenced the drum pattern on her laptop before recording the vocals.

senses.definition: (uncommon) To proceed through a sequence or series of things.
senses.example: The meeting sequenced through budget updates, staffing changes, and a long discussion of parking.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: An ordered series of things or events, or in mathematics, an ordered list of numbers or objects following a rule.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEE. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, and the final syllable is a soft -uns, not a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a general word for order, and in technical contexts a precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sequence in everyday speech to mean the order of events, such as the sequence of steps in a recipe, and in technical contexts for ordered data. In mathematics and data science it has a precise meaning that must be specified. In casual conversation, people often say order or series instead.

distinctions.note: A series usually means things that come one after another, while a sequence emphasizes a specific order that matters.
Order is a more general word for arrangement; sequence specifically refers to the order in which things follow each other.

examples.everyday: The recipe gives the steps in a sequence, so just follow them in order.
examples.professional: We need to check the sequence of the data before we run the model, or the timestamps will be wrong.
examples.analytical: The argument depends on a sequence of premises, and each one must follow logically from the last.

nuance.analogy: Like the beads on a string, where the order they are strung in matters.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sequentia, from sequi (to follow).
common_mistakes: Using sequence to mean a short list or a set, when order matters in the meaning.
Saying 'in sequence' with a different preposition, such as 'on sequence'.
Confusing the noun SEE-kwuns with the verb sequence, which is stressed the same way but used differently.

sequence.etymology: From Middle English *sequence*, from Old French *sequence* (“a sequence of cards, answering verses”), from Late Latin *sequentia* (“a following”), from Latin *sequēns* (“following”), from *sequī* (“to follow”); see *sequent*.

senses.definition: Having tooth-like projections on one side, as in a saw.
senses.example: Many click beetles have serrate antennae.

senses.definition: Of leaves: having tooth-like projections pointed away from the petiole.
senses.example: The leaves of the birch are oval and serrate, with sharp teeth along the margin.

senses.definition: To make serrate.
senses.example: The machinist serrated the edge of the steel blade so it could cut through rope.

senses.definition: To cut or divide in a jagged way.
senses.example: The rocky cliffs serrated the coastline for miles along the bay in jagged, broken outcrops.

core.definition: Having a saw-like edge with many small, sharp, pointed teeth along its border.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final vowel as a clear 'ayt', not 'it'. The r is pronounced in American English, so do not drop it in 'SEHR'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is a precise term rather than an emotional one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serrate mainly in botany, zoology, anatomy and technical description, rather than in casual talk. In everyday speech they would say 'saw-toothed' or 'serrated'. The word is useful in field guides, lab reports and identification keys.

distinctions.note: Serrate is the more technical, precise term, often used for leaf margins, while serrated is more common for knives and everyday objects.
Dentate means having teeth that point outward, perpendicular to the edge, while serrate teeth point toward the tip.

examples.everyday: The leaves on that plant are serrate, so be careful when you brush against them.
examples.professional: In the botany report, describe the leaf margin as serrate rather than just toothed.
examples.analytical: A serrate margin, unlike a crenate one, has pointed teeth that lean toward the leaf tip.

nuance.analogy: A serrate edge works like the blade of a hand saw, with many small points cutting in the same direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin serratus, 'sawlike', from serra, 'saw'.
common_mistakes: Using serrate for everyday objects; Americans usually say 'serrated' for a bread knife.
Adding an extra syllable, saying 'SEHR-ay-tid', which belongs to the adjective serrated, not serrate.

serrate.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *serrātus*, past participle of *serrō*.

senses.definition: A place built alongside a limited-access road where one can stop to buy fuel, refreshments, etc.
senses.example: The sign says that the next service area is 12 miles on.

core.definition: A rest stop beside a highway, usually with fuel, food and restrooms, where drivers can stop for a break.

pronunciation.tip: In an American compound noun the first word gets the main stress, so say SUR-viss, not ser-VISS or the second word. The r in area is clear and the last syllable is a reduced uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes a place for a quick stop, not a social destination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use service area mainly for larger stops on interstates and turnpikes, often with gas stations and fast food. A rest area is usually a simpler stop with restrooms and maybe vending machines but no fuel or food. In Britain the similar facility is called motorway services, which Americans would not say, so say Let's stop at the next service area for a fuel or food break.

distinctions.note: A rest area usually has restrooms and maybe vending machines, while a service area usually also has fuel and food.
Service plaza is a regional term, mainly in the Northeast, for a similar stop, while service area is the broader national term.
A gas station is a business beside the road, while a service area is a complex built along the highway itself.

examples.everyday: Let's stop at the next service area so I can grab a coffee and use the restroom.
examples.professional: The delivery route includes two service areas, so drivers can refuel and log their breaks.
examples.analytical: Highway planners place each service area to balance driver safety, fuel access and traffic flow.

nuance.analogy: A service area is like a pit stop in a race: a short, planned stop for fuel, food and a quick break.
nuance.etymology: Service comes from Latin servitium, and area comes from Latin area, meaning open space.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second word, saying ser-VISS AIR-ee-uh, instead of the first word.
Using service area for a gas station in town, when it refers to a facility along the highway.
Confusing it with service station, which in American English means an auto repair shop or an older gas station.

senses.definition: The mathematical theory of sets.
A systematic approach to describing musical objects and their relationships.
senses.example: Our music theory seminar used set theory to compare atonal pieces by their pitch-class collections.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that studies collections of objects, called sets, and the relationships among them, such as membership, union and subsets.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THE in theory, with a lighter secondary stress on set. The final y is a clear EE sound, and the r in theory is pronounced, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In mathematics and computer science, Americans say set theory without any article in general statements, as in 'I took set theory in college.' The music sense in the dictionary (a method for analyzing pitch-class sets) is specialized and mainly used by music theorists. Outside those fields, most Americans would not recognize the phrase.

distinctions.note: Set theory studies collections and their relations in general, while group theory studies algebraic structures with an operation, such as symmetries.

examples.everyday: My daughter's homework this week was about set theory, and she said it was harder than algebra.
examples.professional: The data pipeline uses set theory logic to remove duplicate records by intersecting the customer ID lists.
examples.analytical: Cantor's work in set theory shows that some infinite sets are strictly larger than others.

nuance.analogy: A set is like a bag of distinct items where the order does not matter and no item appears twice.
nuance.etymology: Theory comes from Greek theōria, meaning 'contemplation' or 'a looking at'; set is an ordinary English word.
common_mistakes: Using set in the everyday sense of a group of things without the mathematical rules of membership and no repetition.
Pronouncing the stress on set, as in SET theory, instead of the more even American stress with the strongest beat on THE.

senses.definition: The state of being severe.
The degree of something undesirable; badness or seriousness.
senses.example: The severity of the offense merits a long prison sentence.

core.definition: How serious, harsh, or bad something is, such as an injury, problem, or punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, VEH, and reduce the first syllable to a short i. The r is pronounced clearly, and the final y is a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes something bad, serious, or harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use severity for medical injuries, storms, crimes, and problems at work. In everyday speech people often say how bad or how serious. Severity is common in news reports and medical contexts but can sound stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Seriousness often describes importance or a solemn attitude, while severity describes how harsh or intense something is.
Intensity describes strength or force, while severity usually describes badness or harshness.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the cut was not serious, so I didn't need stitches after all.
examples.professional: Before we escalate, we should assess the severity of the outage using the incident scale.
examples.analytical: The severity of the sin, in the prophets' account, is measured by the injustice done to the poor.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermometer for trouble: it reads how hot the problem is, not just whether it exists.
nuance.etymology: From Latin severitas, from severus, serious or strict.
common_mistakes: Using severity for seriousness of a solemn person, where seriousness is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the middle one.

severity.etymology: From Middle English *severity*, from Middle French *severite*, from Latin *sevēritās*.

senses.definition: The act or result of something being shaded.
senses.example: the delicate shadings of color in the painted sunset

senses.definition: Something providing shade.

core.definition: Darker tones or areas that show where light is blocked, or the shelter from sun that something provides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable with a long A as in 'shade'. End with a clear -ing, not -een.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical or artistic quality with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shading mostly for drawing, painting, design, and 3D graphics, as in 'add some shading to the sketch.' For sun protection in casual talk, people more often say shade. The word also appears for window coverings and awnings, as in 'the shading on the patio.'

distinctions.note: Shade is the everyday word for a cool, dim, sheltered place; shading is more often the act or result of darkening, especially in art.
A shadow is a specific dark shape cast by an object; shading is the general darkening or tonal method used to show shadows.

examples.everyday: It's so hot out here, so let's sit in the shading from that big oak.
examples.professional: The rendering engine handles shading much better now, so the 3D model looks far more realistic.
examples.analytical: Rembrandt's use of shading creates a moral atmosphere in which the faces seem to emerge from darkness.

nuance.analogy: Shading is like a dimmer on a lamp: it controls how much light reaches each part of a surface.
nuance.etymology: From shade (Old English sceadu) with the -ing ending, forming a noun for an action or result.
common_mistakes: Confusing shading with shadowing, which means following someone closely
Pronouncing the first vowel as a short A, as in 'shad-ing'

senses.definition: Matted material; rough massed hair, fibres etc.
senses.example: The dog's shag of tangled fur needed a thorough brushing after the walk.

senses.definition: Coarse shredded tobacco.
senses.example: He rolled a cigarette with loose shag he bought at the corner shop.

senses.definition: A type of rough carpet pile.
A deliberately messy, shaggy hairstyle.
senses.example: In the eighties he wore a messy shag that fell over his ears.

senses.definition: Any of several species of sea birds in the family Phalacrocoracidae (cormorant family), especially a common shag or European shag (Phalacrocorax aristotelis), found on European and African coasts.
senses.example: Along the rocky Scottish coast, we spotted a shag diving for fish.

senses.definition: A swing dance.
senses.example: At the 1940s dance, everyone was learning the shag between songs.

senses.definition: An act of sex.
senses.example: Their one-night shag left both of them feeling awkward the next morning.

senses.definition: A casual sexual partner.
senses.example: He admitted she was just a shag, not someone he planned to date.

senses.definition: A fundraising dance in honor of a couple engaged to be married.
senses.example: Our friends hosted a shag in honor of the bride and groom before the wedding.

senses.definition: Friend; mate; buddy.
senses.example: Hey shag, are you coming to the game tonight or not?

senses.definition: To make hairy or shaggy; to roughen.
senses.example: The stylist shagged the layers to give her hair a looser, rougher look.

senses.definition: To shake, wiggle around.
senses.example: The toddler shagged to the music, waving his arms and bouncing up and down.

senses.definition: To masturbate.
To chase after; especially, to chase after and return (a ball) hit usually out of play.
senses.example: The outfielder shagged fly balls for an hour during batting practice.

senses.definition: (uncommon) To perform the dance called the shag.
senses.example: Grandma still shags at weddings, though she claims her knees hate it.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: Exhausted, worn out, extremely tired.
senses.example: After the double shift, I was too shagged to cook dinner.

core.definition: A long, rough carpet pile, or a rough, tangled mass of hair or fibers.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short A as in 'cat' and a hard g at the end. Do not add a vowel after the g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for carpet and hair; the verb and slang senses can be vulgar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say shag carpet, shag rug, or shag haircut, the latter a 1970s style. The slang verb meaning to have sex is vulgar and should be avoided in polite company. In baseball, shag refers to chasing fly balls during practice, which is a casual and harmless use.

distinctions.note: Pile is the general term for the surface fibers of a carpet; shag means a particularly long, deep, loose pile.
Fluffy means soft and light; shag suggests rough, long, tangled fibers.

examples.everyday: We have a shag rug in the living room that is so soft it's hard to vacuum.
examples.professional: The hotel lobby uses a low-cost shag carpet, which hides dust but is harder to clean.
examples.analytical: Seventies interior design favored shag texture as a deliberate rejection of sleek modern surfaces.

nuance.analogy: A shag rug is like a field of long grass, soft and tangled instead of flat and smooth.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English shagge, meaning rough or hairy, related to Old English sceacga, a shock of hair.
common_mistakes: Using shag as a casual slang word in front of others, where the verb sense is vulgar
Pronouncing the vowel as a long A, as in 'shade'; it is a short A

shag.etymology: From Middle English **schagge*, from Old English *sċeacga* (“hair, wool”), from Proto-Germanic **skaggô*, **skaggiją* (“projection, bristly hair, stem”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European **kek-* (“to jump, move, hurry”).

core.definition: The name of several people in the Hebrew Bible, most notably a king of Israel who ruled for one month and a son of Josiah who ruled Judah briefly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a quick, reduced uh sound. Non-native speakers often add a long vowel to the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name used in religious study and historical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name almost only in Bible study, sermons, or history classes about ancient Israel. In everyday talk it is not used as a common given name, so people usually add the context, such as the king of Israel or the son of Tikvah.

distinctions.note: Jehoahaz is another name for the son of Josiah who is called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11, so the two names can refer to the same king.

examples.everyday: I always forget which Shallum we're reading about in this chapter, so let's check the verse.
examples.professional: In the study guide, the entry for Shallum needs a note explaining that the name appears for several different people.
examples.analytical: The repetition of the name Shallum in the historical books complicates the chronology and invites careful source comparison.

nuance.analogy: Shallum is like a common family name shared by several relatives in a long genealogy, so the reader must look at the context to know which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: From a Hebrew name meaning he will repay or retribution, from a root meaning to repay.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a long oo sound, as in 'SHAL-oom'.
Assuming Shallum always refers to the same person across the Bible.
nuance.biblical_note: Shallum is the name of several people in the Hebrew Bible. Shallum son of Jabesh reigned briefly over the northern kingdom of Israel in 752 BC, according to 2 Kings 15:10-15 in the Revised Standard Version. Shallum son of Tikvah was the husband of the prophetess Huldah and a keeper of the wardrobe, mentioned in 2 Kings 22:14. Jeremiah 22:11 names Shallum the son of Josiah, who is also called Jehoahaz, as the king of Judah who was taken into exile.

senses.definition: A piece of dining room furniture having drawers and shelves for linen and tableware; originally for serving food.
A board or similar barrier that forms part of the side of something.
senses.example: We stacked the firewood against the sideboard of the old farm wagon before the storm.

senses.definition: A set of cards that are separate from a player's primary deck, used to customize a match strategy against an opponent by enabling a player to change the composition of the playing deck.
senses.example: Before the final round, she swapped three cards from her sideboard to counter her opponent's aggressive deck.

senses.definition: A restriction on using the right to catch a certain number of fish that was granted in relation to a different fishery.
senses.example: The fishing cooperative received a sideboard that allowed its boats to land extra cod from the Gulf.

senses.definition: To include (a card) in one's sideboard.
senses.example: He sideboarded two graveyard cards after losing game one to the reanimator deck.

senses.definition: To add sideboards to.
senses.example: The carpenter sideboarded the old cart so it could haul heavier loads of hay.

core.definition: A long piece of dining room furniture with drawers and shelves, used for storing tableware and for setting out food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SIDE, and let the second syllable be a weak secondary stress. The last syllable has the vowel of caught, not the long o of board, so it sounds like bord with a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a piece of furniture and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sideboard for a long, low cabinet in the dining room, often for serving food at parties or holding dishes and linens. In a furniture store, ask for the sideboard in the dining section. It is not a kitchen counter or cabinet. Buffet and credenza are close alternatives, though a credenza is usually an office piece.

distinctions.note: A buffet in American usage is a dining room serving table; a sideboard is similar but is often built for storage as well.
A credenza is usually an office cabinet, while a sideboard is a dining room piece, though the two can look alike.

collocations: set the food on the sideboard

examples.everyday: We put the cake on the sideboard so the guests can help themselves.
examples.professional: The furniture catalog lists the sideboard in the dining collection, with delivery in six weeks.
examples.analytical: The sideboard, once used to display family silver, became a symbol of middle-class hospitality in nineteenth-century homes.

nuance.analogy: Like a serving station built into the room, always holding what the meal needs.
nuance.etymology: From side, here meaning a side or flank position, plus board, a flat wooden surface.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in side-BOARD; the stress is on SIDE.
Using sideboard for a kitchen counter; a sideboard is a freestanding dining room piece.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of sigmoid function.
Ellipsis of sigmoid colon.
Curved in two directions, like the letter "S", or the Greek ς (sigma); having a serpentine shape.
senses.example: The curve of the river looked sigmoid on the map, bending first one way and then the other.

senses.definition: Exhibiting logistic growth; having a graph that accelerates until it reaches a carrying capacity.
senses.example: Population counts followed a sigmoid curve, leveling off once resources ran short in the lab.

senses.definition: Relating to the sigmoid colon.
senses.example: The surgeon found a small tumor in the sigmoid colon during the routine screening.

core.definition: A mathematical function with an S-shaped curve that maps any input to a value between 0 and 1.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'void'. Do not add an extra syllable, as in 'sig-moy-dee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and AI, 'sigmoid' usually means the sigmoid function, also called the logistic function. Speakers often shorten 'sigmoid function' to 'sigmoid' in meetings and code. The adjective is rare outside medicine or biology, where it refers to the colon.

distinctions.note: Sigmoid gives one probability for a single output, while softmax gives probabilities across multiple classes that sum to one.
ReLU outputs zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive ones, while sigmoid squashes all values into a smooth range from 0 to 1.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI said the output of the model uses a sigmoid to give a probability.
examples.professional: We used a sigmoid activation in the final layer because the model predicts a single yes or no.
examples.analytical: The sigmoid function's smooth, bounded shape allows gradients to be interpreted as probabilities, though it can also cause vanishing gradients.

nuance.analogy: A sigmoid is like a dimmer switch that slowly moves from off to on, rather than snapping between two states.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'sigmoeidēs', shaped like the letter sigma, from 'sigma' and '-oeidēs', having the form of.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sigmoid' with a long 'oy' vowel like 'sig-moyd' with a stressed second syllable.
Confusing the sigmoid function with softmax when discussing multi-class outputs.

sigmoid.etymology: Borrowing from Ancient Greek *σῑγμοειδής* (“of the shape of sigma”), from *σῖγμᾰ* + *-ο-* + *-ειδής*; Equivalent to *sigma* + *oid*.

conversation.text: The sigmoid squashes any real number into the range between zero and one.
We use a sigmoid on the output for binary classification and multi-label problems.
In deep networks, sigmoid activations saturate and make gradients vanish.

senses.definition: The act of simplifying or something that has been simplified.
A valid simple argument.
senses.example: In our logic seminar, simplification lets us conclude P from the premise that P and Q.

core.definition: The act of making something simpler, or a version of something that has been made simpler.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on KAY, with a lighter secondary stress on sim. The -ify- ending of the verb becomes a reduced -uh- syllable in the noun, so do not say sim-pli-fi-KAY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral or positive, since it means making something clearer. It can turn negative when it suggests that important detail was lost.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use simplification in business, science, policy and everyday talk about complicated problems. When a speaker says it is a simplification, they often admit that something important was left out. The stronger word oversimplification signals a clear error in the description.

distinctions.note: Simplicity is the quality of being simple, while simplification is the process of making something simpler or the result of that process.
Oversimplification means the simplification went too far and distorted the truth, so it is almost always negative.

collocations: a simplification of the tax code

examples.everyday: Telling my kids that the sun is a big hot ball is a simplification, but it works for now.
examples.professional: The team agreed that the rollout plan was a simplification of the real dependencies, so we added a review step.
examples.analytical: Every scientific model is a simplification of reality, and its value depends on which details it keeps and which it discards.

nuance.analogy: A simplification is like a subway map: it drops the exact street curves to show you how to get from one station to another.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin simplificare, from Latin simplex ('simple') and facere ('to make').
common_mistakes: Using simplification to mean simplicity, as in 'the simplification of the design is good' when you mean its simplicity.
