nuance.connotation: Usually negative, suggesting an excessive or unhelpful emotional reaction. It can be neutral when describing excitement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Don't get worked up' to calm someone down, and 'Why are you so worked up?' when someone is overreacting. It is casual conversation, not formal writing. A natural reply is 'Sorry, I'm just stressed about it.'

distinctions.note: Upset is a general word for distress and is neutral in tone, while worked up suggests a buildup of agitation or excitement.
Agitated is more formal and describes visible restlessness or anxiety, while worked up is casual and conversational.
Irate means very angry and is stronger, while worked up can describe anxiety, excitement or anger.

examples.everyday: Don't get all worked up about the parking ticket; we'll just pay it online.
examples.professional: The client was worked up about the delay, so let's call them before the meeting.
examples.analytical: Public debates often become so worked up that participants stop weighing evidence and simply defend their group identities.

nuance.analogy: Being worked up is like a kettle that starts whistling before the water is really hot: the reaction is louder than the situation.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb work up, meaning to stir up or excite someone's feelings.
common_mistakes: Adding 'of' after worked up; use 'worked up about' or 'worked up over' instead.
Pronouncing the -ed as a separate syllable, 'work-ed up'; the ending is just a t sound.

senses.definition: Of a person, the period of their life spent in employment, between leaving school and retirement.
senses.example: Her working life spanned four decades at the same hospital.

senses.definition: Of an object, its lifespan, especially a durable good; its expected duration or its actual duration.
senses.example: Cheaper tires typically have a shorter working life than the pricier alternatives, which means that the total cost of ownership (per mile) is closer to equal although the upfront cost is more affordable.

core.definition: The years of a person's life spent in paid employment, from finishing school until retirement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIFE, with WORK lighter. The diphthong in life is long, /aɪ/, and the final f is voiceless, not a v.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound reflective or respectful, especially when someone talks about a career or legacy. It describes a span of time, not an achievement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'during my working life' or 'over the course of my working life' when reflecting on a career. For machines or products, US engineers usually say service life or useful life, though working life appears in some technical writing. Do not use it in casual talk to mean the time you spend at your job on a given day; say 'my job' or 'work.'

distinctions.note: A career is the path or profession you pursue; working life is the total period of time you spend in paid work, whatever the career.
Lifetime is the whole length of a life; working life covers only the years in paid employment.
Service life is the technical term for how long an object is expected to last; working life is the everyday term for a person and sometimes an object.

collocations: the rest of her working life
the end of one's working life

examples.everyday: I worked at the same hospital for most of my working life, so retiring still feels strange.
examples.professional: The pension plan rewards employees for contributions made across their whole working life, not just their final years.
examples.analytical: Economists measure working life to compare earnings and labor participation across generations, but the category hides the career breaks that many people take.

nuance.analogy: Like the active seasons of an athlete's career: a defined stretch between starting out and stepping away.
nuance.etymology: From working plus life; working describes activity and life describes the span of existence.
common_mistakes: Using working life to mean a single job; it refers to the whole span of paid work.
Confusing it with work-life balance, which is a separate idea about dividing time between work and personal life.

senses.definition: To write at full length or in expanded form.
senses.example: Don't use abbreviations; write out words!

senses.definition: To write or fill out (a ticket or citation).
senses.example: The officer wrote out a speeding ticket before handing me my license back.

senses.definition: To exclude from a narrative or history.
senses.example: Historians have long complained that the textbooks wrote out women scientists entirely.

senses.definition: To remove (a character in a fictional series such as a TV show) by writing the script so as to explain their disappearance (through death, moving away, etc.).
senses.example: The writers wrote out the sitcom's popular neighbor with a plane crash.

senses.definition: To exhaust one's mental capacity by too much writing.
senses.example: After grading essays all night, I felt completely written out by morning.

core.definition: To write something in full, without abbreviations, or to fill out a form, ticket, or check completely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'out', the particle of this phrasal verb. The w is silent, and the 'ow' sound is a diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes careful, complete writing and has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'write out' for writing the full version of something, such as 'write out the full name' or 'write out the steps.' In traffic or police contexts, Americans say 'write a ticket' more often, though 'write out a ticket' is also used. In TV talk, 'write out a character' means to remove a character from a show, which is common in American entertainment news.

distinctions.note: 'Write down' means to record something quickly, often in short form, while 'write out' means to write the complete version.
'Fill out' is used for forms and applications, while 'write out' is used more for full text, steps, or the complete version of something.

examples.everyday: Could you write out the directions for me? Your handwriting is hard to read on the back of this receipt.
examples.professional: Please write out the full acronym on the first slide so the executives know what the abbreviation means.
examples.analytical: The author writes out the argument step by step, so that every premise can be checked before the conclusion is accepted.

nuance.analogy: Writing out is like unfolding a folded map: the shortened version is folded up tightly, and writing it out opens every panel so the whole picture is visible.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb built from 'write' and the adverb 'out', meaning to put something fully into writing.
common_mistakes: Using 'write out' for quick notes; 'write down' is the better choice for a short record.
Saying 'write out a ticket' when talking about giving a parking ticket in everyday speech; 'give a ticket' is also common in American English.

senses.definition: In violation of a moral or other standard, code, or convention; in an unfair, unjust, dishonest, or immoral manner; wrongly convicted is synonymous with wrongful conviction and miscarriage of justice.
senses.example: The jury wrongly convicted him of robbery, and he spent eleven years in prison.

senses.definition: Incorrectly, mistakenly; by error.
senses.example: I wrongly assumed that it would be an easy job.

core.definition: Incorrectly or by mistake, or in a way that is unfair or immoral.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ng is a single nasal sound, and the final ly is a light, quick ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a simple error or an unjust act, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wrongly for simple mistakes such as wrongly labeled or wrongly assumed, and for unjust actions such as wrongly convicted. In casual speech people often say by mistake or incorrectly. It is widely used in news and legal contexts.

distinctions.note: Incorrectly is neutral and technical; wrongly can also imply moral fault or injustice.
Wrongfully is stronger and more legal; wrongly is broader and can describe simple error.

examples.everyday: I thought the restaurant had closed, but I was wrongly informed by the website.
examples.professional: The report wrongly listed the server as offline, so the team lost an hour checking the wrong system.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that we wrongly treat moral intuition as if it were a complete account of justice.

nuance.analogy: Wrongly is like a clock set to the wrong time: it is not broken, but every reading it gives is off.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wrang, meaning twisted or wrong, with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using wrongly where a more natural everyday phrase like by mistake would fit better.
Stressing the second syllable.
Confusing wrongly with rightly, its opposite.

senses.definition: Turned away, contorted (of the face or body).
senses.example: She made a wry face when the bitter coffee hit her tongue.

senses.definition: Dryly humorous; sardonic or ironic, usually in a way that suggests acknowledgement of a problem or difficult situation.
senses.example: Her wry comment about the broken printer made the whole team laugh.

senses.definition: Twisted, bent, crooked.
senses.example: The old oak had a wry trunk, bent by decades of coastal winds.

senses.definition: Deviating from the right direction; misdirected; out of place.
senses.example: His wry attempt at a joke landed badly during the serious budget meeting.

senses.definition: To twist or contort (the body, face, etc.).
Distortion.
senses.example: The warped mirror's wry made her face look strangely stretched and unfamiliar.

core.definition: Dryly humorous in a way that shows you notice something absurd or unpleasant, often with a slight smile.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long i, so it sounds like the grain 'rye.' Keep the r rhotic, pronounced clearly before the vowel, and do not add a y sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive. It suggests clever, understated humor, sometimes with a hint of resignation about a bad situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wry' to describe a smile, a look, or a comment that is funny but a little sarcastic or ironic. You might say 'She gave a wry smile when the meeting ran late again.' It is not usually used for loud or obvious jokes.

distinctions.note: Sarcastic remarks are often meant to hurt or mock, while wry remarks are gentler and mainly show dry amusement.
Ironic describes a gap between what is said and what is meant or happens; wry describes the dry, knowing tone of the speaker.

examples.everyday: He gave me a wry smile and said, 'Well, there goes our lunch break.'
examples.professional: Our project lead made a wry comment that the deadline had been moved again, and everyone laughed.
examples.analytical: Her essay adopts a wry tone that exposes the gap between the church's ideals and its everyday practice.

nuance.analogy: A wry smile is like a small crack of light in a serious room: it shows humor without breaking the mood.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'wrye,' meaning twisted or bent, from Old English 'wrigian,' to turn.
common_mistakes: Using 'wry' to mean a loud or openly funny joke.
Confusing the pronunciation with 'Y' or 'why.'

wry.etymology: From Middle English *wrien*, from Old English *wrīġian* (“to go, turn, twist, bend, strive, struggle, press forward, endeavor, venture”), from Proto-Germanic **wrigōną* (“to wriggle”), from Proto-Indo-European **wreyḱ-* (“to turn, wrap, tie”), from **wer-*…

senses.definition: Knowledge of a language one has never learned.
Glossolalia.

core.definition: Supposed knowledge or speech of a language one has never learned, often linked with Pentecostal speaking in tongues.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GLAH, and the final -y is a long EE sound. Start with ZEN, not ZEE, and keep the g hard as in 'go'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a technical term; often used skeptically when discussing claims of supernatural ability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in discussions of parapsychology, religion, and language research. In everyday talk, people usually describe the idea in plain words, such as 'she spoke a language she never studied'. Writers often use it to ask whether a claim is real, so expect a skeptical or investigative tone.

distinctions.note: Glossolalia is ecstatic speech that usually has no recognizable grammar or vocabulary, while xenoglossy claims an intelligible known language.
A polyglot has learned several languages through study; xenoglossy is the claimed ability to know a language without learning it.

examples.everyday: Some people at church call it xenoglossy when someone prays in Swahili, but I think she'd just heard a lot of it at work.
examples.professional: The video was flagged as a possible xenoglossy case, so we sent the recording to a linguist for review.
examples.analytical: Anyone defending xenoglossy must show that the speaker could not have acquired the language by ordinary means.

nuance.analogy: Xenoglossy is like hearing a song you never learned and singing every word back perfectly, with no record of ever having heard it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek xenos (foreign, stranger) and glōssa (tongue, language).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with glossolalia, which is unintelligible ecstatic speech rather than a known foreign language.
Saying the first syllable as 'zee'; the correct sound is ZEN.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is modern, but Scripture describes related phenomena. In Acts 2:4-11, at Pentecost, the disciples speak in languages that visitors from many nations understand, which is closer to xenoglossy than to glossolalia. In 1 Corinthians 14:2, Paul describes one who speaks in a tongue as speaking to God, since no one understands him. The Greek glōssa means tongue or language.

traditions.view: Orthodox teaching links the Pentecost gift to the Spirit uniting people across languages in the Church. Tongues are regarded as a gift to be discerned and ordered within the Church's worship and discipline, not as a required sign.

The Catholic Church recognizes speaking in tongues as one of the charisms described in 1 Corinthians 12, but it does not treat it as a necessary sign of receiving the Spirit. Such gifts are to be discerned and used to build up the Church.

Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians see speaking in tongues as a continuing gift, sometimes as initial evidence of Spirit baptism. Reformed cessationists hold that the sign gifts ended with the apostolic age, while Lutheran and Anglican views are generally more reserved.

senses.definition: The action of the verb yawn.
senses.example: His constant yawning during the sermon made it clear he had stayed up too late.

senses.definition: That yawns or yawn.
senses.example: yawning commuters

senses.definition: Wide open.
senses.example: a yawning chasm; the shark's yawning jaws

core.definition: Very wide and open, like a deep gap or chasm that seems to have no bottom.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, YAWN. The -ing ending is a short, unstressed 'ing' sound, not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or threatening. It suggests a dangerous or empty space, and is often used for a big problem or difference.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'yawning gap' or 'yawning chasm' in writing and speech to describe a large difference, such as between two groups or between a plan and reality. It is more figurative than 'wide,' so use it when you want to suggest danger or emptiness. Speakers often use it in news, politics and business talk.

distinctions.note: Gaping means wide open, often in a visible hole, while yawning emphasizes an emptiness that seems deep and threatening.
Vast describes large size or scale, while yawning suggests a dangerous or empty opening.
Wide is a neutral physical description, while yawning is figurative and emotionally charged.

examples.everyday: Careful, there's a yawning crack in the sidewalk right by the curb.
examples.professional: We have a yawning gap between our forecast and actual sales, so we need to rebuild the model.
examples.analytical: The essay exposes a yawning gap between professed belief and daily practice in the congregation.

nuance.analogy: A yawning gap is like the open mouth of a cave: you can see the edge, but not how far down it goes.
nuance.etymology: From yawn (verb) and the -ing participle ending, describing something that is open wide.
common_mistakes: Using 'yawning' to mean 'tired' or 'sleepy' in a literal way; in English it describes a wide opening or gap.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a long 'eeng' rather than a short 'ing'.

senses.definition: Synonym of yes way.
senses.example: Yeah way, you finished the whole marathon with a broken toe?

core.definition: Informal American way of saying yes enthusiastically, meaning definitely or absolutely, often used to accept an offer or agree strongly.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on WAY and say yeah as a quick, open sound. Speak the two words together as one fast phrase, not as two separate words.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals eager agreement, though a flat tone can make it sound sarcastic.
nuance.usage_note: Young Americans and friends use this among themselves in casual speech, such as when someone suggests plans. In professional settings or with older people, plain 'yeah' or 'definitely' sounds more natural. A natural reply is 'Cool, I'll text you the address.'

distinctions.note: 'No way' is the opposite, expressing refusal or disbelief, so mixing them up reverses your meaning.

examples.everyday: Want to grab tacos after class? Yeah way, I'm starving.
examples.professional: Can you take the client call Thursday? Yeah way, I can handle it.
examples.analytical: Her reply to the critique was simply 'yeah way,' which signaled quick agreement without any real argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a high-five delivered in words: quick, warm, and enthusiastic.
common_mistakes: Using it in formal emails or meetings, where it sounds too casual
Confusing it with 'no way', which means the opposite

senses.definition: Bare or universal life.
senses.example: In the seminar, we debated whether zoe in John's Gospel refers to eternal life.

senses.definition: An instance of getting zoed.
senses.example: Paying three hundred dollars for that fake watch was a total zoe.

senses.definition: To cheat someone out of money, to rip off.
senses.example: The salesman zoed my cousin out of two hundred dollars for a used laptop.

core.definition: In theology and philosophy, the basic fact of life itself, as contrasted with bios, a particular way or form of living.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as two syllables with the stress on the first, ZOH, and a clear ee at the end. Do not say it as one syllable like 'zow', which is a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and academic. In theological settings it can carry a sense of gift or fullness of life, but it is not a warm everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use zoe almost only in theology, philosophy and classical studies, usually borrowed from Greek. In everyday English, people say life, and they do not use zoe in casual talk. The slang verb meaning to cheat someone is rare and informal, and most Americans say rip off or scam instead.

distinctions.note: Zoe refers to life itself, while bios refers to a form or course of a life, as in biography or biology.
Life is the everyday English word, while zoe is a technical term used to draw a theological or philosophical distinction.

collocations: zoe in the Gospel of John

examples.everyday: My Greek professor said zoe means more than just breathing, and that helped me understand the Gospel.
examples.professional: In our ethics seminar we distinguished zoe from bios when we discussed end-of-life policy.
examples.analytical: John's Gospel uses zoe for the life that the Son gives, a life shared with God rather than mere biological existence.

nuance.analogy: If bios is the story of a life, like a biography, zoe is the living ink that the story is written with.
nuance.etymology: From Greek zōē, meaning life.
common_mistakes: Using zoe as a casual synonym for life in everyday conversation.
Confusing zoe with bios, which is a different word for a form or course of life.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word zōē means life in its fullest sense, the living reality that God gives, as distinct from bios, the form or course of a life. John 1:4 says that life was in the Word and was the light of people. John 5:26 says the Father has life in himself and has given the Son to have life in himself. John 14:6 names Christ as the life along with the way and the truth.

zoe.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ζωή* (“life”), first distinguished in this particular sense by Giorgio Agamben.

core.definition: A Jewish governor of Judah under Persian rule who led exiles back from Babylon and helped rebuild the temple.

pronunciation.tip: The name is spelled Zerubbabel in the Revised Standard Version, which Americans usually read; Zorobabel is the Douay-Rheims spelling. Stress falls on RUB, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a weak 'buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive as a figure of faithful leadership in the return from exile. As a name it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: In American English the standard spelling is Zerubbabel, following the RSV. You may see Zorobabel in older Catholic Bibles or the Douay-Rheims version, so recognize it as the same person. Americans mostly meet the name in sermons, Bible classes and seminary study of Ezra, Haggai and Zechariah.

distinctions.note: Zerubbabel was the civil governor who led the first return from Babylon, while Ezra was a priest and scribe who came later with his own group of returnees.

collocations: Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher said the people under Zerubbabel had a hard time rebuilding the temple after they came home from Babylon.
examples.professional: For the sermon, I'll use the story of Zerubbabel to show how God works through modest beginnings and does not need great power.
examples.analytical: Haggai's oracle to Zerubbabel presents the governor as a signet ring, a sign of divine authority restored to the Davidic line after the exile.

nuance.analogy: Like a foreman who finishes a building long after the first blueprint was drawn, Zerubbabel carried the project across decades of delay.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Zerubbavel, usually explained as seed of Babylon, though the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying the name with stress on the wrong syllable, such as zer-oo-BAH-bel.
Confusing Zerubbabel with Ezra, the priest and scribe who came to Jerusalem later.
nuance.biblical_note: Zerubbabel, Hebrew Zerubbavel, is the governor of Judah who leads the Jewish return from Babylonian exile and works with Joshua the high priest to rebuild the temple. Ezra 3:2 shows him with Jeshua the priest rebuilding the altar. Zechariah 4:6-7 says that the work is accomplished not by might or by power but by God's Spirit, a message delivered to Zerubbabel. Haggai 2:23 promises that God will make Zerubbabel like a signet ring, a sign that he has been chosen. Matthew 1:12-13 and Luke 3:27 list him in the genealogy of Jesus.
